builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: LLM Agent-Based Design of RISC-V CPUs with FPGA-in-the-Loop Evaluation
summary: The method replaces hours-long RTL simulation as the feedback signal for LLM-agent-guided CPU design with on-board FPGA performance measurements of synthesized candidates. It costs FPGA implementation time per candidate, requires physical Artix-7-class hardware and a synthesis toolchain, and adds human supervision over the agent loop. It can fail when designs do not fit the target FPGA, when synthesis results diverge from ASIC-relevant timing, or when board-level measurements mask RTL bugs that simulation would expose.
rationale: The technique targets RTL/CPU hardware development with physical FPGA boards, which is outside the production scope of an AI/ML engineer working with a single 24 GB GPU or inference APIs.
technique: FPGA-in-the-loop evaluation for LLM-agent CPU design

claims.statement: The method replaces hours-long RTL simulation as the feedback signal for LLM-agent-guided CPU design with on-board FPGA performance measurements of synthesized candidates. It costs FPGA implementation time per candidate, requires physical Artix-7-class hardware and a synthesis toolchain, and adds human supervision over the agent loop. It can fail when designs do not fit the target FPGA, when synthesis results diverge from ASIC-relevant timing, or when board-level measurements mask RTL bugs that simulation would expose.

For one CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation including implementation was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation, and the final three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core reached 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on an Artix-7 FPGA.
